Sixth grade science · Unit 4

Weather & the Water Cycle

The water in your glass has been rain, ocean, cloud, and ice before. Weather is the atmosphere moving that water around, powered by the Sun. By the end of this page you can explain why it rains, why the wind blows, and why Ann Arbor isn't Miami.

Where we left off: sunlight (Unit 1) is absorbed and becomes thermal energy (Unit 2), and heated air and water move in loops called convection. You may already have learned that warm fluids rise and cool fluids sink. That is what powers weather, and forces (Unit 3) such as air pressure and gravity steer it.

Concept 1 · The atmosphere

An ocean of air

Air has mass. The atmosphere is a stack of layers, and the higher you go the thinner the air and the lower the pressure.

Analogy

A stack of blankets

The bottom blanket is crushed by everything on top. Air near the ground is packed tightly (high pressure); air at the top is loose (low pressure).

Try it

Rise through the atmosphere

Data

Pressure drops fast as you climb

Half of all the air is below about 5.5 km. Pressure is measured in hectopascals (hPa); sea level is about 1,013 hPa. Rounded teaching model.

Concept 2 · The water cycle

The same water, over and over

The Sun's energy drives the cycle: evaporation lifts water up, condensation makes clouds, precipitation brings it down, and collection sends it back. No water is made or lost.

Analogy

Your bathroom after a hot shower

Steam rises

Hot water turns to gas: evaporation.

Mirror fogs

Steam hits the cold mirror and turns to droplets: condensation.

Drips run down

Droplets get heavy and fall: precipitation.

That mirror is a tiny water cycle. The Sun does the same job for the whole planet.

Diagram

The whole cycle

Try it

Will the cold glass sweat?

Data

Where is Earth's water?

ocean (salty) 97ice and glaciers 2groundwater 1

Out of every 100 drops of Earth's water, about 97 are in the oceans. Lakes and rivers are less than one hundredth of one drop. We rely on a very small slice. (Rounded; groundwater is partly salty.)

Concept 3 · Pressure and fronts

Why the weather changes

Weather changes when air masses of different temperature and pressure meet. A falling barometer usually means a storm is coming, and a front is where two air masses collide.

Analogy

A crowded gym and an empty gym

People spread from the crowded room to the empty one. Air does the same: wind blows from high pressure toward low pressure.

Diagram

Cold front vs. warm front

Data

Three days, one storm

Made-up but realistic data for a cold front passing through. Warm before the front (southwest wind), then a sharp drop in temperature, rising pressure, and clearing after.

Concept 4 · Why the wind blows

Sun heats ground unevenly

Land warms and cools faster than water. The warm air over land rises, cool air from the water rushes in, and that is a sea breeze. At night the pattern flips.

Analogy

A pan and a pot of water

Same sunshine, same minute. The pan (land) gets hot fast; the pot of water (ocean) barely warms. Water needs about four times as much energy as rock or soil to warm up, so it heats and cools slowly. Now add air: air over the hot pan rises, and cooler air from over the pot slides in to replace it. That sliding air is the sea breeze. At night the pan cools faster, the pattern flips, and the breeze blows the other way.

Where it breaks: a beach is not a stove. The Sun heats the ground from above and the ocean is deep, so the real ocean stores far more heat than a pot.

Try it

Beach through the day

Data

Land swings, water barely moves

The wind blows from whichever is cooler toward whichever is warmer. They cross around mid-morning and evening, and the breeze switches. Teaching values.

Real world

Michigan examples

EventExplanation
Cool breeze off Lake Michigan on a hot dayLand is warmer than the lake; air rises over land and lake air flows in.
Lake-effect snow in West MichiganCold air crosses warmer lake water, picks up moisture, then cools over land and drops it as snow.
Lake keeps the shore mild in fallWater releases its stored thermal energy slowly.
Build it

Engineering challenge: the cup anemometer

The problem: build a spinning anemometer that counts wind speed by how fast it turns in front of a fan.

Criteria: spins freely, and gives roughly the same count (within 2) on two tries at the same fan speed.

Constraints: 4 small cups, 2 straws, 1 pencil, a pin or paperclip for the axle, and tape.

  1. Try it in the game first. Play Droplet's Journey at the bottom of this page. Notice how the wind keeps pushing in one direction.
  2. Plan. Sketch two different ideas on your design log. Think about why the cups all face the same way and why the pivot needs to spin with as little friction as possible.
  3. Build and test. Count rotations for 20 seconds at low fan speed, then at high fan speed. Repeat each speed once to check your count.
  4. Improve. Change one thing, test again, and record it.

Print a design log for each team. Real anemometers use this exact idea: count spins in a fixed time, and faster wind means more spins.

Concept 5 · Weather vs climate

One day vs. thirty years

Weather is what the atmosphere is doing today. Climate is the pattern over many years, usually 30 or more. Climate tells you what to pack; weather tells you what to wear today.

Analogy

Mood vs. personality

One grumpy Tuesday doesn't make someone a grumpy person. One cold day doesn't change the climate. Climate is the average of thousands of days, just as personality is the pattern across thousands of moods.

Data

Average monthly temperature (°F)

Approximate 30-year monthly averages. One hot April day is weather. It does not move the line, which is climate.

Diagram

The greenhouse effect

Sunlight passes through the air and is absorbed by the ground. The warm ground gives off invisible heat rays. Greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide and water vapor absorb some of those rays, then give the energy off again in every direction, so part of it heads back down. Nothing is sealed in like a lid: heat still escapes to space, just more slowly. Without any, Earth's average would be about -18 °C (0 °F) instead of about 15 °C (59 °F).

Real world

Weather or climate?

Check yourself

Can you explain it?

Explain why a breeze blows off the lake on a hot afternoon, and how the lake is part of the water cycle.

Show a model answer

Land heats faster than water, so air above land warms, expands, and rises, leaving low pressure. Cooler air from the lake flows in to fill the gap, which is the breeze.

The Sun evaporates lake water into water vapor. High in the air it cools and condenses into clouds, and then falls as rain or snow that runs back into the lake: evaporation, condensation, precipitation, collection.

0 of 6 correct

Words to know

atmosphere
The layer of gases around Earth.
air pressure
The push of air's weight on everything below it.
evaporation
Liquid water turning into water vapor.
condensation
Water vapor turning into liquid droplets.
precipitation
Water falling as rain, snow, sleet, or hail.
dew point
The temperature at which air gets so cool that water vapor condenses.
front
Boundary between two air masses.
sea breeze
Daytime wind from cool water to warm land.
weather
Atmosphere conditions at a place and time.
climate
Typical weather pattern over 30 or more years.
Tutor notes: hands-on kit, misconceptions, pacing

Kit (about $10): a clear jar, ice, hot water, hairspray or a match for the cloud-in-a-jar demo, a metal can, a balloon, a bottle, thermometers, sand and water in two trays, a lamp. For the cup anemometer: 4 small cups, 2 straws, a pencil, a pin or paperclip, and a fan.

  • Concept 1: blow up a balloon, tie it, put it in a bag, and squeeze: air takes up space and presses back. A quick balloon-on-bottle barometer works.
  • Concept 2: make a cloud in a jar with hot water, a plate of ice on top, and a squirt of aerosol. Sweat a cold can.
  • Concept 3: record pressure from a weather app each hour for a day.
  • Concept 4: put sand and water under a lamp and compare temperatures every minute for 10 minutes. Then run the cup anemometer challenge (about 30 to 40 minutes).
  • Concept 5: print a month of daily highs for your town and draw the average line.

Common misconceptions:

  • "Clouds are made of smoke or cotton." They are billions of tiny water droplets or ice crystals.
  • "Rain comes from clouds holding all the water at once." It falls when droplets collide and get heavy.
  • "Cold weather today disproves climate change." It confuses weather with climate.
  • "The greenhouse effect is bad." It's natural and necessary. The concern is adding too much.
  • "Greenhouse gases put a lid on the heat." They absorb heat rays and send some back down; heat still leaves for space, just more slowly.

Pacing: about five 30-minute sessions.

Play: Droplet's Journey

Guide one water molecule from Lake Michigan to a garden in Ann Arbor. Every step of the water cycle only works when the conditions are right, and the wind keeps pushing you east.
